jar.name: Her labdanum jar
jar.about: Labdanum softens and deepens as it rests. Start a jar now: it has to age for 60 game days (about nine real days) before it's ready.

brief.memory: Her own perfume, the one she never sold. The last page of her book, nearly blank. Everything the town, her growers and her book have told you comes together here.
hints: Bright for a moment, then soft.
Roses kept in a powder box, over an old resin and a little sweetness.

clues.text: She wore something of her own on Sundays. Bergamot first, like my cologne, but it never stayed bright for long.
Under hers was the same warm resin she gave my wife, only softer and sweeter.
Forty years of her letters, and every envelope smelled faintly of lavender. Just a whisper.
My mother always said Mireille smelled like roses kept in a powder box.
She bought a few grams of our rose every year and never sold a drop. 'For the shop,' she wrote.
She asked for the oldest gum we had, and kept it in a jar for a long time before she used it.
Only ever a little of our lavender for herself, she said. Never the main thing.
Her own order never changed: vanillin in the brown bottle, a little at a time.
On the back of the wedding page, in pencil: 'Mine starts like this one, then turns to the garden.'
A note beside the winter amber: 'Same resin in mine, but aged. Never fresh.'
Under Lucien's formula: 'The roundness is the vanilla, as in mine. Equal to the resin.'
An old entry: 'Mireille, passed. Brought an accord built on Florentine iris; asked to keep the recipe.'

epilogue.title: The last page
opening: You write it down at last, in your own hand, under her title: For the shop.
The town comes by over the next weeks, one by one, to smell it. Some of them cry. Most of them just smile and say, 'There she is.'

byPath.town: You found her through the people who loved her: their weddings, their winters, their Sundays. The shop was always theirs as much as hers.
byPath.routes: You found her through the growers: the groves, the fields and the hills that sent her their best for fifty years. Their letters still come, and now they're addressed to you.
byPath.craft: You found her through the work itself: her pages, her margins, the exams she sat before you. You learned her trade the way she did, one material at a time.

epilogue.pages: {pages} of her pages are whole again, and the rest are waiting.
epilogue.style: Your shop has its own character now: it leans {style}, and the customers who love that keep coming back.
epilogue.closing: The book isn't finished. It never was. You turn to a clean page and start your own.
